name: Frankfurt plane

card.summary: A standard head-orientation line (ear canal to lower eye socket rim) used to level the head when judging or photographing a facial profile, so profile comparisons are fair.
card.aka: Frankfurt horizontal; Frankfort plane; FH plane
card.note: A measurement convention; head tilt in a photo changes how the profile reads.

quick.overview:
The Frankfurt plane is a reference plane defined by two landmarks: the lower edge of the eye socket (orbitale) and the top of the ear canal (porion). When the head is held so this line is level with the ground, profile features such as the forehead, nose and chin can be compared on a consistent basis.

For appearance, it matters because a head tilted up or down in a side photo changes how recessed or projected the jaw, chin and forehead look. Looksmaxxing forums use it to take and read profile photos, and orthodontists and surgeons use it in cephalometric analysis.
quick.how: In forum use, people photograph or draw their side profile with the head oriented so the line from the ear canal to the lower orbital rim is horizontal, then check features against vertical lines dropped from landmarks. Threads often ask others whether a photo is correctly aligned.
quick.risks: No physical risk; the main limitation is measurement error. Researchers have examined how reliable landmarks and head posture are, and some dental researchers have proposed alternative reference planes.

lead: The Frankfurt plane, also called the Frankfurt horizontal, is a standard reference plane for the human head. It passes through the lower margin of the left eye socket (orbitale) and the upper margin of each ear canal (porion), and was agreed at an anthropology congress in Frankfurt am Main in 1884 as the plane most nearly parallel to the ground when the head is carried naturally [10].

In looksmaxxing, the plane is used to standardize profile photos and facial analysis. Because the angle of the head changes how the forehead, midface and chin line up, members ask whether a side photo is on the Frankfurt plane before judging features such as chin projection or forehead position [7][9]. Some posters use vertical lines from landmarks dropped relative to the plane to discuss recession, and some ask what surgical changes would be needed to change a profile measured this way [8].

Outside forums, the plane is used in orthodontics, prosthodontics, craniofacial surgery and physical anthropology, where it orients skull and head measurements. Studies of cephalometric methods have tested its reliability against other references [5][3].

chain: Head leveled to ear-canal and lower-eye-rim line
Profile photo comparable between people and over time
Chin, nose and forehead position read accurately
angle.text: It does not change the face; it standardizes how a profile is photographed and measured. People use it to check their own profile fairly and to describe what a surgeon or orthodontist would be correcting.

infobox: Orbitale (lower orbital rim) and porion (top of ear canal)

paras: The plane is defined by three points: the left orbitale and the two porions. Three points fix a plane in space, which is why the convention is convenient for orienting skulls and living heads [10].
Anthropologists compare human skulls with those of primates by orienting them to this plane, although it is not horizontal in the natural posture of most non-primate species [10].

sections.h: Use in clinical and research settings
paras: Orthodontists use cephalometric tracing to analyze incisor position, jaw relationships and vertical facial pattern, and reference planes are central to those measurements [1][2][4]. Dental researchers have proposed substitutes such as the SIDS plane as alternatives to the Frankfurt horizontal [3].

Studies have examined head posture and photographic versus radiographic orientation [11], reliability of 3D cephalometry measured relative to the plane [5], and primate head posture used to evaluate registration planes in paleoanthropology [6].

On looksmax.org, threads ask whether a user is correctly aligned, how lines from the nasal bridge or forehead relate to the chin, and what to do when features sit behind the line. One user describes that even with the chin sculpted, the line still does not touch it, and others reply that alignment advice such as lifting the head slightly so the ear-canal top matches the lower orbital rim is part of getting an accurate photo [7][9].

In a thread about a forehead lying behind the line, one commenter says that changing it would require moving the whole forehead forward or the lower face back, and defers to a surgery-focused member [8]. Community members treat profile analysis this way as a way to describe skeletal recession and projection.

No studies found on the plane as a looksmaxxing tool. Clinical and anatomical research on reference planes, head posture and cephalometric measurement exists in orthodontics and surgery [1][2][5][11].

timeline.event: The Frankfurt plane is adopted at an anthropology congress in Frankfurt am Main as the standard orientation of the skull [10].

lore.intro: Forum members use the Frankfurt plane as the standard for profile photos and for judging recession of the chin, midface and forehead [7][9].

claims.claim: A profile photo is only meaningful if the head is on the Frankfurt plane
claims.believers: Posters say that tilting the head up or down changes how recessed or forward features look, so photos must be aligned before analysis [9].
claims.experts: Orthodontic literature treats reference plane and head posture as important sources of measurement variation and has tested alternatives [11][3].

claims.claim: A line from the nasal bridge or forehead shows how recessed the chin is
claims.believers: Members draw lines from landmarks to the chin to judge recession and discuss surgery to correct it [7][8].
claims.experts: Cephalometric research uses defined landmarks and angles, and studies compare measurement methods for reliability [1][5].
